meta.name: Same Whole
meta.title: Adding fractions with different denominators
meta.subtitle: Make the pieces the same size before you add them.

tutor.name: Mika
tutor.welcome: We'll take this one line at a time. You do the thinking; I'll help when you need a nudge.

explain.heading: Why can't we add them yet?
explain.intro: A denominator tells you how many equal pieces make one whole. Thirds and quarters are different-sized pieces, so adding them straight away would be like adding centimetres to inches.

blocks.heading: Find a common denominator
blocks.body: Look for a number both denominators divide into. The smallest one is usually easiest. It gives both fractions the same-sized pieces.

blocks.heading: Rename each fraction
blocks.body: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same number. The fraction keeps its value; only the way it is written changes.

blocks.heading: Add, then simplify
blocks.body: Once the denominators match, add the numerators and keep the denominator. If the answer can be reduced, divide the top and bottom by the same common factor.

explain.remember: The denominator stays the same when you add. The numerators are the parts you add.

workedExample.heading: Watch: 2/3 + 1/4
workedExample.intro: Watch the whole method. Each line appears when you're ready for it.

steps.label: Find a common denominator
steps.math: 3 and 4 both divide into 12, so use 12.
steps.spoken: The smallest number that both 3 and 4 divide into is 12.

steps.label: Rename the first fraction
steps.spoken: Multiply the top and bottom by 4. Two thirds becomes eight twelfths.

steps.label: Rename the second fraction
steps.spoken: Multiply the top and bottom by 3. One quarter becomes three twelfths.

steps.label: Add the numerators
steps.spoken: The pieces are now the same size. Add 8 and 3, and keep the denominator 12.

steps.label: Check whether it simplifies
steps.math: 11/12 is already in its simplest form.
steps.spoken: Eleven and twelve have no common factor greater than one, so the answer is finished.

workedExample.finish: So, 2/3 + 1/4 = 11/12. The important move was making the pieces the same size first.

together.heading: Let's do one together
together.intro: This time, you enter each line. Use the fraction boxes for the top and bottom numbers. I'll check the maths, not just the final answer.

steps.label: 1. Find a common denominator
steps.question: What number can both 2 and 6 divide into?
steps.hint: List a few multiples of 6. Which one is also a multiple of 2?
steps.correctFeedback: Yes. 6 works for both denominators, and it is the smallest common denominator.
steps.largerFeedback: That works too: both original denominators divide into it. The smallest common denominator is 6, which keeps the numbers simpler.
steps.wrongFeedback: Not quite. A common denominator must be divisible by both 2 and 6. Try a multiple of 6.

steps.label: 2. Rename the first fraction
steps.question: Write an equivalent fraction for 1/2 using your common denominator.
steps.hint: Ask: 2 multiplied by what gives your common denominator? Multiply the numerator by that same number.
steps.correctFeedback: Exactly. You multiplied the numerator and denominator by the same number, so the value stayed the same.
steps.wrongDenominator: Use the common denominator you chose in the previous line. The denominator must match before the fractions can be added.
steps.wrongNumerator: The denominator is on track. Multiply the original numerator by the same factor you used for the denominator.
steps.wrongFeedback: Check that the new fraction has the same value as 1/2 and uses your chosen common denominator.

steps.label: 3. Rename the second fraction
steps.question: Now write an equivalent fraction for 1/6 using the same denominator.
steps.hint: If 6 already matches your common denominator, does this fraction need to change at all?
steps.correctFeedback: Right. This fraction has been rewritten with the same denominator and still has the same value.
steps.wrongDenominator: Both renamed fractions need the same denominator. Use the common denominator from line 1.
steps.wrongNumerator: The denominator is right. Check how many times the original denominator was multiplied, then do the same to the numerator.
steps.wrongFeedback: Check that the new fraction has the same value as 1/6 and uses your chosen common denominator.

steps.label: 4. Add the numerators
steps.question: Add the two numerators. Keep the common denominator for now.
steps.hint: Add the numbers on top only. Do not add the denominators.
steps.correctFeedback: Yes. Add the numerators and keep the common denominator unchanged.
steps.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Add the two numerators from the previous lines. The denominator does not change when you add fractions with matching denominators.

steps.label: 5. Simplify the answer
steps.question: Write the final answer in its simplest form.
steps.hint: Look for a number that divides evenly into both the numerator and denominator. Divide both by that same number.
steps.equivalentNotSimplified: That fraction has the right value, but it can still be simplified. Divide the numerator and denominator by their highest common factor.
steps.wrongFeedback: Check that your final fraction has the same value as the fraction you made in line 4, then see whether it is fully simplified.
steps.correctFeedbackTemplate: That’s it. {from} reduces to {to} because you divide the top and bottom by {factor}.

together.completion: You made the pieces the same size, added the numerators, and simplified. That's the full method.

independent.heading: Your turn
independent.intro: Work through one line at a time. Only the line you are answering is shown; your completed working stays visible above it. Hints are available whenever you need one.

steps.label: 1. Find a common denominator
steps.questionTemplate: What number can both {leftDenominator} and {rightDenominator} divide into?
steps.hint: List multiples of each denominator. Look for a number that appears in both lists. The smallest common one usually keeps the working simpler.
steps.correctFeedbackTemplate: Correct. {value} is the smallest common denominator.
steps.largerFeedbackTemplate: That is a valid common denominator. {smallest} is the smallest one, so it keeps the working simpler.
steps.wrongFeedback: The number must be divisible by both original denominators. Try another multiple.

steps.label: 2. Rename the first fraction
steps.questionTemplate: Write {leftFraction} as an equivalent fraction using your common denominator.
steps.hint: Find the multiplier that takes the original denominator to your common denominator. Multiply the numerator by that same amount.
steps.correctFeedbackTemplate: Correct. {fraction} has the same value as {original}.
steps.wrongDenominator: Use the common denominator you chose in line 1.
steps.wrongNumerator: Multiply the numerator by the same factor you used for the denominator.
steps.wrongFeedback: Check that the fraction keeps the same value and uses your common denominator.

steps.label: 3. Rename the second fraction
steps.questionTemplate: Now write {rightFraction} using the same denominator.
steps.hint: Compare the second denominator with your common denominator. If they already match, the numerator may not need to change.
steps.correctFeedbackTemplate: Correct. {fraction} has the same value as {original}.
steps.wrongDenominator: Both renamed fractions must use the common denominator from line 1.
steps.wrongNumerator: Multiply the numerator by the same factor you used for the denominator.
steps.wrongFeedback: Check that the fraction keeps the same value and uses your common denominator.

steps.label: 4. Add the numerators
steps.questionTemplate: Add the two numerators. Keep the common denominator unchanged.
steps.hint: Add the numbers on top only. The denominator stays the same because the pieces are now equal in size.
steps.wrongFeedback: Add the two numerators only. Keep the denominator unchanged.

steps.label: 5. Simplify the answer
steps.questionTemplate: Write your result as a fraction in its simplest form.
steps.hint: Look for the greatest number that divides evenly into both the numerator and denominator. Divide both by it.
steps.equivalentNotSimplified: The value is right, but it is not in its simplest form. Divide the numerator and denominator by a common factor.
steps.wrongFeedback: Check that your final fraction has the same value as the sum from line 4.

independent.completion: You completed every line. The numbers changed, but the method stayed the same: find a common denominator, rename both fractions, add, then simplify.

answerRules.commonDenominator: Any positive common multiple of both denominators is accepted, up to 10,000.
answerRules.equivalentFractions: The learner must enter an equivalent fraction and use the common denominator selected in the first line.
answerRules.addition: The learner must add the converted numerators and keep the shared denominator.
answerRules.finalFraction: Any mathematically equivalent fraction in lowest terms is accepted.
